extracted.intended_audience: researchers, instructors, and authors in undergraduate mathematics education (RUME community)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for types of conference submissions to RUME and for designing/evaluating creativity-based mathematical tasks used in undergraduate mathematics instruction and research. Covers submission categories, review expectations, conference themes, and concrete task features that foster mathematical creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributed Research Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributed Research Reports describe completed research studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended for full, completed studies; submitted papers in this category should present finished research with results and analysis suitable for conference presentation and inclusion in proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary Research Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary Research Reports describe ongoing research projects in early stages of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this category for work-in-progress where data collection or analysis is incomplete but promising; suitable for getting feedback from the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical Research Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical Research Reports describe new theoretical perspectives for research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended for papers developing or proposing theoretical frameworks, conceptual analyses, or substantial reconceptualizations relevant to undergraduate mathematics education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poster Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Posters are 1-page summaries of work that was presented in poster format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for succinct summaries, pilot studies, replication reports, or work best communicated visually; limited length/format expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each submission underwent a rigorous review by two or more reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions are evaluated through multi-reviewer peer review; authors should prepare work to meet scholarly standards and address likely reviewer concerns (clarity, methods, contributions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference thematic fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions should align with the conference themes: results of current research, contemporary theoretical perspectives and research paradigms, and innovative methodologies and analytic approaches as they pertain to undergraduate mathematics education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing submissions, emphasize fit to one or more themes; highlight research contribution, theoretical framing, or methodological innovation as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple solutions / multiple representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks that afford multiple solutions and multiple representations were used most frequently and are seen as a feature that fosters mathematical creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that allow more than one correct answer or more than one representational approach (algebraic, graphical, numerical, verbal). These are feasible entry points to promote creativity and were commonly used by instructors in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended feature: tasks without a single correct answer or that ask students to create/choose functions meeting criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-ended tasks can foster creativity and additional mathematical processes (e.g., written communication). Study participants used open-ended features less frequently, so special attention may be needed in design and implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different approaches leading to one answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks structured so different approaches can lead to the same answer (the feature was utilized but minimally by participants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include prompts where students can use diverse methods (algebraic manipulation, limits techniques, geometric reasoning) to converge on an agreed solution; encourages comparison of approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making connections between concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks that promote making connections between different ideas and concepts (noted as commonly fostered by participants' tasks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design prompts that require or reward linking multiple mathematical ideas; explicit prompts or rubric elements that value connections can highlight this feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-posing and student-generated questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks that ask students to pose problems and questions (problem-posing) were identified as an important creativity feature though used less often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include activities asking students to generate their own problems, examples, or conjectures; such tasks can uniquely afford creative thinking but may require scaffolding and classroom norms for success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation / justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks that explicitly ask students to evaluate or justify their answers or approaches (justification coded as important/most common for some instructors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require explanation, proof, or critique as part of the task to develop justification skills; in implementation, follow-up discussion and questioning can deepen this feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written mathematical communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Using tasks as a writing assignment to provide practice in written mathematical communication (example: telling students there is not a single correct answer and having them write about it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate written responses into tasks to build communication skills; clarify expectations and grading criteria for explanations in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incubation / outside-class work
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation strategy: assign tasks to work on outside class and bring results back for discussion (incubation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use out-of-class incubation to allow longer reflection and development of creative solutions; include structures to ensure follow-up discussion and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment integration (exam inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether creativity-based tasks appear on major assessments (e.g., final exams) — observed that some instructors included creativity tasks on exams while others did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including creativity-based tasks on high-stakes assessments signals their importance and can increase student engagement; however, instructors may need to align grading rubrics and provide practice opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sriraman's five principles for teaching practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching practices aligned with Sriraman's five principles (Gestalt, Uncertainty, Free Market, Scholarly, Aesthetic) have potential to foster students' creativity. Gestalt and Uncertainty correspond to task features; Free Market, Scholarly, and Aesthetic correspond to aspects of implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both task design (e.g., gestalt/uncertainty features such as open-endedness and emergent structure) and implementation climate (free exchange of ideas, scholarly norms, aesthetic appreciation) to meaningfully promote creativity. These implementation aspects differentiate creativity-based tasks from mere non-routine tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple-solution tasks as an entry point
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentional selection or creation of tasks that have multiple solutions or that can be approached in different ways is a feasible entry point into fostering mathematical creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For instructors new to emphasizing creativity, begin by altering tasks to allow multiple solution paths and representations before moving to more open-ended or problem-posing designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task feature triangulation (design/implementation/interview/journal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangulate task design, instructors' journal reflections, and interview transcripts to validate which features were emphasized and how implementations played out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When researching or reporting on task effectiveness, use multiple data sources (task artifacts, teaching journals, interviews, assessments) to support claims about what features fostered creativity.
